events.excerpt: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and wh
events.headline: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm

events.excerpt: Fused filament fabrication (FFF, also known as FDM) 3Drinting specialist InfiMech has opened crowdfunding for an eight-toolhead 3D printer family, the MX Series — promising "near-zero waste" multi-color and multi-material printing. "Unlike traditional single-nozzle systems that purge material during every single color swap, the InfiMech MX Series utilizes a smart independent tool architecture," InifiMech's Xingshuai Xiong explains of the new printer family. "Each tool purges only once upon its first activation to ensure the melt zone is perfectly filled. Subsequent color switches require no further filament waste throughout the entire print. Printing an eight-color model produces only eight small purge drops in total — reducing material waste and printing time to the absolute minimum." Multi-toolhead printers, contrasted with automatic material switchers, aren't a new concept — but at the cheaper end of the market you're usually limited to four toolheads in total. The InfiMech MX, by contrast, comes with six as standard while the MX Pro moves to eight. events.excerpt: It’s hard to believe how lucrative this crime can be: According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men ­ Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit ­ were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026. With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money. The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. Always remember that there are three parts of AI security: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. This is the third.
events.headline: Three People Arrested for AI-Enhanced Impersonation Fraud

Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. events.excerpt: The following is an opinion post reflecting my vision for a possible design direction for Ethereum, not a concrete design. What I argue for is to rethink the notions of scaling, availability, and finality according to the principles of elasticity. TL;DR Ethereum’s capacity is configured in advance: one block per slot, a fixed slot time, a gas limit and a size limit. Price matches demand to it, and safety margins cover for the network. No protocol-wide rule adapts capacity limits to measured resource pressure. Elasticity is first of all about robustness. An elastic system measures what it can carry and takes on less when it is falling behind. A system without that feedback is the kind that goes into congestion collapse, and Ethereum’s overload incidents look like it. Scaling comes with it. A system that can back off can afford to run close to what the network and the nodes can carry, where a fixed margin has to pay for the worst day every day. TCP is the working example: its congestion control was built to stop collapses, and it is also much of why the same protocol, with small changes, runs on modems and on fibre. events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: clea
events.headline: Cosmup: install, switch and check Cosmos chain binaries (like nvm, for gaiad/osmosisd/...)

events.excerpt: Why is crypto crashing on Wednesday, November 11? The sell-off that began with Tuesday’s hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation report has carried into today, and almost every major coin is lower. Bitcoin (BTC) dropped below $73,000 on Tuesday, touching $72,727 on Binance, and now trades at about $73,800. Ether (ETH) briefly slipped to $2,006, while XRP and Solana (SOL) are down 2% to 3% in 24 hours. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, a daily gauge of market mood from 0 to 100, has fallen to 29. events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it.
